The situation

Two of everything, and one of each drifting

See the detail

Your plant crushes about 120,000 tonnes of ore a day at about 0.55% copper. The ore goes through two grinding lines, then two flotation lines dosed with lime, collector and frother. The concentrate is about 28% copper. It is thickened, filtered on two filters and trucked to port by the wet tonne.

The waste rock slurry goes through two tailings thickeners to a conventional dam. A reclaim barge pulls water back from the dam to a process water tank, and four pumps send it around the plant. Fresh water comes by pipeline from a desalination plant. After power, it is your largest cost you can control.

Most of the findings come from twin units: two filters, two thickeners and two flotation lines that treat the same material. Where one twin does worse than the other, the cause sits inside that unit or in how it is run.

Most large concentrators are in this position. The control system holds each loop on its setpoint, and each unit is individually reasonable. What it does not do is notice that one of two thickeners now sends far more water to the dam, or that one line holds a pH the other proves it does not need. Water is where most of the money sits, because every cubic metre lost has to be bought and pumped up from the coast.

The approach

Find the loss, find the cause, price it, confirm it

See the detail

AquaMesh does not assume a fixed percentage. It starts from the plant's existing control-system and historian data and works through five steps.

01Detect

141 measuring points were read from the plant's own records. Every unit was compared with its identical twin, day by day, across 150 days, and every flow and power figure was held up against a balance.

02Diagnose

Each symptom was tested against what the instrument measures and how it typically misleads, to separate process problems from instrument problems. They resolved into 4 causes and 1 reading that needs a field check.

03Price

Each cause was priced from measured quantities, the plant's own curves and its own unit costs, against its own best comparable unit, never a design figure.

04Route a response

Each cause became one specific action with an owner and a timing. AquaMesh recommends; operators decide. Nothing is actuated.

05Verify

Each cause carries a metric and a target, tracked against a baseline from this same record, normalised for load and weather.

CAUSE 1

Thickener 2 sends 355 m³/h more water to the tailings dam than it needs to

$3,235,950/yrmeasured

Thickener 2 and thickener 1 thicken the same tailings. Thickener 1's underflow leaves at 64.5% solids; thickener 2's has fallen from 63.1% to 59.0%, since its bed level was taken down from 3.1 m to 1.6 m on 24 May. Water that leaves in the underflow goes to the dam instead of straight back to the process water tank. The plant's own record shows how much of it comes back: of each extra cubic metre sent to the dam, 54% returns through the reclaim barge about a day later. The rest evaporates off the beach and pond, and is replaced with bought water.

reclaim against water sent, 1-day lag, R² 0.94, 147 days

What it means

The change lines up with the date the bed was lowered, so the evidence points to a deliberate change, not a faulty instrument. The water clarity is the same on both thickeners, so the lower bed has not cost you a cleaner overflow. What it has cost is water sent out to the dam, where part is lost and replaced with bought water. The first step is to find out who made the change and why.

What the operator does

Restore thickener 2's bed level toward 3.1 m once the cause of the torque alarm is cleared, and bring its underflow back toward thickener 1's 64.5% solids.

How it is confirmed

Thickener 2 underflow solids and site fresh-water draw. Target: about 64.5% solids; fresh water down about 165 m³/h at the same ore rate.

CAUSE 2

Line 2 uses 42% more quicklime per tonne than line 1, for no more copper

$1,355,449/yrmeasured

Line 2 and line 1 treat the same ore. Line 2 uses 1.09 kg of quicklime per tonne; line 1 uses 0.77. The difference is the pH it is held at: 11.00 against 10.55. Lime demand climbs steeply with pH, so the last few tenths cost the most. Recovery is 90.0% against 90.1%, so the extra reagent is not buying copper.

What the data shows

same ore
Rougher pH
11.00 vs 10.55

Copper recovery
90.0 vs 90.1 %
no gain for the extra reagent

What it means

Line 2 is held at a higher pH than line 1, and the copper recovery is the same on both. The extra lime is therefore not buying you more copper. Lime use climbs fast at the top of the pH range, so a small step down should save more than you might expect. Left alone, you keep paying for a reagent that gives nothing back.

What the operator does

Bring line 2's rougher pH setpoint down to line 1's 10.55 in two steps over a week, and watch copper recovery and concentrate grade at each step.

How it is confirmed

Line 2 quicklime per tonne and copper recovery. Target: about 0.77 kg/t with recovery unchanged.

CAUSE 3

The process water pumps run flat out against their own valves

$474,274/yrmeasured

The process water pumps run at full speed and hold the header pressure by choking their discharge valves, which sit at about 47% open and take 205 kPa out of the water. Measured at the pump terminals the pumps turn 78% of their electricity into pressure and flow; 27% of the power is then burnt across the valves. A variable-speed drive or a trimmed impeller gives the same header pressure without it.

What the data shows

Valve position
47 % open
duty pumps, daily average
Pressure across the valves
205 kPa
a control valve needs about 30 kPa
Pump electrical to hydraulic
78 %
at the terminals
Power burnt across valves
811 kW
692 kW above the minimum

What it means

The pumps are doing more work than the plant needs, and the valves waste the surplus as heat. The pumps themselves are in good shape. The loss comes from how pressure is held. Left alone, that power is wasted every hour the pumps run, and a variable-speed drive or a trimmed impeller would remove most of it.

What the operator does

Fit variable-speed drives on the duty process water pumps (or trim impellers) and control header pressure on speed, leaving the valves near fully open.

How it is confirmed

Process water pumps: kWh per cubic metre delivered. Target: about 0.210 kWh/m³ at the same header pressure.

How the value is built

Pump power burnt across discharge valves, above the minimum a valve needs692 kW × 8,059 h$0.085/kWh$474,274
Total$474,274
CAUSE 4

Filter 2 ships more water in its concentrate than its twin

$359,812/yrmeasured

Filter 2 and filter 1 filter the same concentrate. Filter 1 holds 8.4% moisture; filter 2 has drifted from 8.5% to 10.1%. Freight is paid on wet tonnes, so every point of moisture is water shipped at concentrate rates, and it moves the cargo closer to its moisture limit for shipping.

What the data shows

Filter 2 cake moisture

Filter 1 cake moisture
8.4 %
same feed
Dry solids through it
44.34 t/h
weighed, dry basis
Extra wet tonnes
22.3 t/day
7,496 t a year

What it means

Filter 2 is making wetter concentrate than its twin from the same feed, so the problem sits inside that filter and not in the feed. The data cannot say which part is at fault. A worn cloth or a weak seal are candidates, and the filter's own records point the same way. Left alone, you keep paying freight on water, and the cargo moves closer to its shipping moisture limit.

What the operator does

Inspect filter 2's cloths and squeeze cycle, and match its cycle settings to filter 1's.

How it is confirmed

Filter 2 cake moisture. Target: 8.4% moisture.

One finding is not counted

They are shown because they are worth acting on this week. A meter error is money only once you know which meter is wrong; a safety finding has no price, and should not need one.

LEAD

The two pipeline meters have separated by 2.4%

up to $1.4M/yrmeasurednot counted in the total

The two meters on the pipeline agreed at the start of the record and now differ by 2.4%. It is a steady slide, not a process change, because a real change in flow would move both. An independent meter on the same water agrees with meter B to within 0.1%; meter A reads 2.4% high. Meter A is the supplier's: it is the one the water bill is paid on.

What the data shows

Meter A against meter B
1.000 → 1.024

Meter A against the reference
+2.4 %

What the error is worth
$1,391,794/yr
the error on the water bill, at the delivered price

What it means

A third, independent meter agrees with meter B, so the evidence points to meter A reading high. It is the one the supplier bills on. Until it is checked, you pay for water that never reaches your tank. The slide has been steady, so the gap will probably keep widening.

What the operator does

Verify meter A against a portable reference before it is used again for the monthly water bill.

How it is confirmed

The two meters and the reference. Target: within 1% of each other.

Sensors

Where the water hides the money, a probe shows it

See the detail

Everything above came from instruments the plant already owns. What none of them can see is what the recycled water carries back to flotation: residual collector, sulfur salts and organics that move recovery on both lines at once. AquaSpectra sits in the pipe and reads the water's spectral fingerprint continuously, and learns against the plant's own flotation and laboratory results what a change means.

Where each probe goes, what it sees, and what it is worth

Process water to flotation

The plant sees today

conductivity and pH on the process water tank, which see salts but not the reagents and sulfur salts that come back in recycled water.

AquaSpectra adds

It reads residual collector, sulfur salts and organics in the water going to the cells, as a change in the ultraviolet spectrum, learned against your own flotation results.

How the value is counted

  1. Recovery both lines lose together, beyond grade and grind: 0.09 points on average, against the best tenth of days
  2. Copper in the feed: 27.5 t/h, so $1.6M/yr is at stake at $8,600/t net payable
  3. We assume water explains half of it and the reading lets the plant act on half of that
  4. Counted: a quarter, $411k/yr

Is it right?

The audit was checked against the plant's own truth

See the detail

This plant is a physical simulation, built so the answer is known. Four faults were built into it. The audit read only the historian export, the way it would read yours, and priced what it found. The simulator was then re-run with each fault removed, on the same weather and the same load, and the difference priced at the same unit costs. The audit never saw that.

Built-in faultSimulator truthAudit foundAudit ÷ truth
Thickener 2 thin underflow$2,968,668$3,235,9501.09
Line 2 lime overdose$1,353,561$1,355,4491.00
Filter 2 cloth blinding$333,645$359,8121.08
Process water pumps throttled$474,271$474,2741.00
Total$5,130,145$5,425,4851.06

The sensor estimate was checked too. The simulator says the hidden water-quality driver cost the plant $776k a year of copper. The audit, which cannot see it, put $1.6M at stake from the recovery record and counted a quarter of that, $411k: about 53% of the true loss, which is the share a probe that lets operators act on half of it would be worth.

The same plant with every fault removed audits at $0 of direct savings. Where the audit sits below the truth it is because it counts conservatively (a median night, a stated minimum valve pressure); where above, it is the twin it was compared with running slightly better than the fault-free plant would.
